## What

`notifySyncInvalidate(name, args?, data?)` has a **90-second
source-side dedupe window**. Two notifies with identical
`(name, args, data)` fired within that window: the second one is
silently dropped before `pg_notify` runs.

The dedupe now lives in the **generic** invalidation bus
(`libs/generic/sync/src/server/invalidation-bus.ts`, `@papercusp/sync/server`),
not in the operator's `sync-sse.ts`. `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts`
is now a thin wrapper that injects the operator's PG transport into
`createInvalidationBus()` and re-exports `notifySyncInvalidate` (=
`bus.notifyInvalidate`) unchanged — the path moved from `apps/operator/lib/sync-sse.ts`
→ `packages/operator-core/lib/sync-sse.ts` and the mechanism was
generalized, but the contract is identical.

The constant:

```ts
const DEFAULT_DEDUPE_WINDOW_MS = 90_000;  // 90 seconds (opts.dedupeWindowMs override)
```

This sits IN the producer, before the channel write. SSE
subscribers never see the dropped event. There's no log line; the
suppression is intentional.

## Why it exists

The 60-second `harness-fs-watcher` reconcile sweep upserts every
(slug, panel) row every minute even when nothing changed. Without
this guard, the operator fires ~80 no-op notifies per minute and
the dashboard's panels refetch in lockstep, which renders as
constant flicker.

The window is sized just over the reconcile interval so a *real*
per-minute change still gets through (the preceding no-op notify
falls out of the dedupe map by then).

## When this is a footgun

You add a new heartbeat / per-tick notify expecting clients to
refetch every tick:

```ts
// every 5 seconds (this is wrong):
setInterval(() => {
  void notifySyncInvalidate('myStream.recent').catch(() => {});
}, 5_000);
```

Result: clients refetch ONCE, then nothing for 90 seconds. The
17 dropped notifies in between go nowhere. You spend an hour
wondering why the UI is stale.

## How to bypass the dedupe (when you actually want every notify)

The dedupe key hashes `(name, args, data)`. Vary any of them
per call:

```ts
// Option 1: include the timestamp in args
void notifySyncInvalidate('myStream.heartbeat', { ts: Date.now() });

// Option 2: include a sequence number
void notifySyncInvalidate('myStream.heartbeat', { seq: ++heartbeatSeq });

// Option 3: carry the actual data payload (data-bearing notifies
// hash the data into the dedupe key, so a NEW row set passes
// through naturally)
void notifySyncInvalidate('myStream.recent', undefined, latestRows);
```

For data-bearing notifies the dedupe documentation says:
> Notifies with a `data` payload are never dedupe'd — they carry
> actual content and the receiver acts on them, not just refetches.

That's not quite right: data-bearing notifies ARE dedupe'd, but
the data hash is in the key, so a different payload bypasses.
Identical payloads (rare but possible) still dedupe.

## How the dedupe map lives

```ts
const recentNotifies = new Map<string, number>();
```

**Update (post-generalization):** the dedupe map is now a plain
module-scoped `Map` captured in the `createInvalidationBus()` closure
(`libs/generic/sync/src/server/invalidation-bus.ts`). It is **no longer
pinned to `globalThis.__syncNotifyDedupe`** — that idiom existed to
survive Turbopack/Next HMR, and the operator no longer runs the bus
inside the Next dev request path (operator is a Vite SPA + Hono host;
the Hono host runs under `tsx` with no HMR). The bus is a single
long-lived instance created once at module load, so a closure Map is
sufficient. (A stale `delete globalThis.__syncNotifyDedupe` line still
lingers in `sync-sse.test.ts` cleanup but is a no-op against the closure
Map.) `ensure-schema.ts` — the other place this idiom was used — has
since been removed entirely (schema is migrations-only now).

## The PG-trigger producer (P-018) does NOT use this dedupe

The PG trigger `emit_change_notify` writes to the same
`sync_invalidate` channel but **does not** go through
`notifySyncInvalidate`. It calls `pg_notify` directly from the
trigger function. So the 90s dedupe applies only to app-code
notifies.

This is fine in practice: the trigger fires on real PG writes,
not on heartbeats. If an app write triggers the PG row update AND
calls `notifySyncInvalidate`, the trigger fires first (synchronous
inside the txn), the app-code notify second; identical (name, args)
collisions get caught by the consumer-side `last-event-id` semantics
+ the listener's own internal handling.

## Capacity

`recentNotifies` is bounded — when it exceeds 200 entries,
`pruneNotifyCache` walks the map and drops entries older than the
90s window. Cheap GC; no unbounded growth on long-lived processes.

200 is sized for ~one notify per (panel, slug, phase) across
registered harnesses. If you blow past it you're probably also
hitting other problems.
